steps: Import NumPy as np — that alias is the convention every reader expects.
Pass a Python list to np.array; the values decide the dtype.
Read shape and dtype before printing values, so the data's structure is explicit.
Create your first array.visual:
list:  [10, 20, 30, 40]
         ↓ np.array
array:  [10 20 30 40]   shape (4,)  dtype int64
Create your first array.realWorld: A shop's daily sales arrive as a Python list; converting it once to an array makes the total, average and best day single calls instead of loops.
mistakes: Calling np.array() with no argument — it needs a sequence.
Comparing a list and an array with == and expecting a single True/False; NumPy returns an elementwise mask.
revision: np.array(sequence) → one typed, contiguous ndarray.
shape is the structure, dtype is the element type, and both are printed for free.

steps: Write the arithmetic expression for one element, not a loop over elements.
Pass the array where the single value stood.
Print the result's shape to confirm it preserved the input shape.
Vectorised arithmetic.visual:
a        = [1 2 3]
a * 2    = [2 4 6]     one compiled pass, no Python loop
Vectorised arithmetic.realWorld: Converting a column of prices from dollars to rupees is one multiplication by the exchange rate, applied to every row at once.
mistakes: Writing a Python for loop anyway, which pays interpreter overhead per element.
Expecting an in-place change — the expression returns a new array.
revision: Vectorised code describes the whole array, not one element.
The result is a new array with the same shape.

steps: Create the array and read dtype.
Multiply itemsize by size to confirm nbytes.
Create the same data as float64 and compare nbytes.
Typed memory, not a Python list.visual:
int64  : 8 bytes × 5 = 40 bytes
float64: 8 bytes × 5 = 40 bytes
int8   : 1 byte  × 5 =  5 bytes
Typed memory, not a Python list.realWorld: A million-row sensor log fits in 8 MB as float64 and 1 MB as int8 when the readings are small whole numbers.
mistakes: Assuming a Python list's memory is its element count — the list also stores pointers.
Downcasting without checking range, which silently wraps values.
revision: nbytes = itemsize × size.
dtype is a memory decision as well as a precision decision.

Two arrays combine elementwise.syntax: a + b   |   a - b   |   a * b   |   a / b
steps: Confirm both arrays have the same shape.
Apply the operator; positions pair up.
Check the result shape matches the operands.
Two arrays combine elementwise.realWorld: Adding yesterday's per-product sales to today's gives a per-product total, without touching product names or order.
mistakes: Expecting [1 2 3 10 20 30]; that is concatenation.
Mixing shapes that cannot broadcast and reading the error as a data problem.
revision: Arithmetic pairs positions, it does not append.
Shape errors are checked before the data is.

steps: Count from zero to reach the first element.
Use a negative index to count from the end.
Slice with start:stop to take a range, remembering stop is excluded.
Indexing starts at zero.realWorld: The first and last reading of a day are a[0] and a[-1]; the morning block is a[0:6].
mistakes: a[4] on a 4-element array — out of bounds, not the last element.
Expecting a[1:3] to include index 3.
revision: Zero-based, negative counts from the end.
Slices exclude the stop index.

steps: Call the reduction method directly on the array.
Print the value and its type to see it is a NumPy scalar.
Pass axis when the reduction should collapse only one dimension.
Methods return plain results.realWorld: A dashboard needs one best score and one total; both come from methods, not loops.
mistakes: Calling the Python builtin sum(a) and losing dtype and speed.
Using axis on a 1-D array and expecting a different number.
revision: Reductions return scalars unless axis is given.
The method form is the vectorised one.

steps: Call tolist() on the array.
Check the result contains native ints/floats rather than NumPy scalars.
Pass that list to the API or JSON encoder that needed it.
Convert back to a Python list.realWorld: A JSON endpoint cannot serialise an ndarray; tolist() is the one-line boundary fix.
mistakes: Believing tolist() changes the original array — it returns a copy.
Serialising the array directly and getting a TypeError.
revision: tolist() is a copy to plain Python containers.
Use it at the boundary, not inside numerical code.

steps: Inspect dtype for an integer list and a float list.
Try storing 2.5 in an integer array through astype and observe truncation.
Choose float64 when fractions must survive.
Integers and floats carry different dtyp.visual:
[1 2]      dtype int64    → cannot hold 2.5
[1.0 2.0]  dtype float64  → holds 2.5
Integers and floats carry different dtyp.realWorld: Marks out of 100 are integers; a percentage average is a float, and mixing them silently truncates unless the dtype is chosen deliberately.
mistakes: Assuming astype rounds — it truncates toward zero.
Building an integer array from sensor decimals and losing the decimals.
revision: dtype is inferred from the values.
Cast deliberately, and round before casting if precision matters.

steps: Write the expression with the scalar.
Confirm the shape did not change.
Change the scalar and re-run to see it applied everywhere.
Add a scalar to every element.realWorld: Adding a fixed delivery fee to every order in a day's array is one addition.
mistakes: Looping to add the same number.
Expecting an in-place update; a new array is returned.
revision: Scalars broadcast across the whole array.
This is the smallest example of broadcasting.

steps: Compare the array with the threshold to get a boolean array.
Pass that mask back into the array to select the matching values.
Count with mask.sum() when only the number matters.
Compare an array with a scalar.realWorld: Filtering students who scored above 80 is one comparison plus one index.
mistakes: Writing if a > 10: — a multi-element array has no single truth value.
Forgetting the mask must match the array's shape.
revision: Comparisons return a mask, not a bool.
The mask selects; it does not modify.

A Python loop still works over an array.syntax: for value in a:   |   for row in matrix:
steps: Iterate to see what one step yields (element for 1-D, row for 2-D).
Compare the loop result with the vectorised expression.
Keep the loop only where per-element control flow is genuinely needed.
A Python loop still works over an array.visual:
1-D: each step → element
2-D: each step → whole row  [1 2 3]
A Python loop still works over an array.realWorld: Printing a formatted line per row is a fair use of a loop; summing a million values is not.
mistakes: Using a loop for arithmetic that has a vectorised form.
Assuming iteration over a 2-D array gives single numbers.
revision: Iteration walks the first axis.
Loops are for control flow, not for bulk arithmetic.

steps: Check the type after np.array.
Try calling a list method on the array and read the error.
Convert explicitly with np.asarray or tolist at the boundary.
Every array reports its own type.realWorld: A helper that accepts either a list or an array should call np.asarray once at the top instead of branching everywhere.
mistakes: Checking type(a) == list for an array.
Assuming np.matrix is the modern return type — it is legacy.
revision: np.array always returns ndarray.
Normalise inputs at functions' edges.

steps: Sum a list with Python's builtin to see the loop-based path.
Convert to an array and use the method.
Compare the code shape: one expression versus a loop plus accumulator.
Why NumPy exists.visual:
Python:  loop → add → append   (interpreter per element)
NumPy :  one call over the buffer (compiled)
Why NumPy exists.realWorld: A CSV with a million prices is summed in milliseconds as an array and in noticeable seconds as a Python loop.
mistakes: Assuming NumPy is faster for a handful of values — the constant cost can dominate.
Assuming every operation is faster; dtype conversions still cost.
revision: NumPy's win is compiled, contiguous, homogeneous work.
Measure before claiming a speedup.

steps: Build an array from mixed values.
Read the dtype to see the promotion.
Build a list with the same values and note it keeps each type.
An array versus a list.visual:
list : [1, 2.5, True]   types kept
array: [1.  2.5 1. ]   dtype float64
An array versus a list.realWorld: A column read from a spreadsheet is one type; NumPy enforces that, which is why cleaning happens before the array is built.
mistakes: Mixing text and numbers and losing the text to a string dtype.
Assuming True stays a separate boolean beside floats.
revision: Arrays are homogeneous; lists are not.
Promotion is silent — check dtype after building.
